title: Oscar and the Regiment
premise: In the winter of 1813, Jude Kavanagh works as a nurse in a regimental workshop town on a frozen river, quietly recording in her ledger the names of common soldiers that officers leave out of official dispatches. When an officer's aide abandons a child at her door with orders to forget his face, Jude realizes the boy is evidence of something powerful men want erased, and her ledger becomes both shield and target. As spring thaws approach and the regiment prepares to burn its records and move on, Jude races to finish documenting every name while protecting the child from the colonel who ordered him forgotten. The book ends with the ice breaking: the workshop burns as planned, but Jude's ledger survives, smuggled out by the found family she has gathered, and she chooses to stop being invisible, signing her own name at last.
about_author: Elodie Ishikawa is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military hospital records before turning to fiction. She writes about the people history files under 'miscellaneous,' and lives near a river that freezes every winter.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Establishes the workshop hospital on the frozen river, her nightly ritual of recording names officers omit from dispatches, and her belief that history happens elsewhere. Emotional beat: quiet defiance disguised as routine.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. During a blizzard, an aide leaves a mute boy of about six at her door with coins and the instruction to forget his face. She takes him in against regulation. Emotional beat: fear curdling into reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: What the Colonel Ordered
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, with a scene from Sergeant Brannigan's POV. Rumors circulate about a dead lieutenant and an inquiry the colonel wants closed quickly. Jude suspects the child is connected. Emotional beat: dawning unease.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Will Not Speak
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. She names the boy Oscar and coaxes him with food and mending work; he draws faces obsessively, including one in a fine coat. Emotional beat: tenderness breaking through her guardedness.

chapters.title: Visitors
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth's POV. The colonel inspects the workshop, notices the boy, and questions Jude with velvet menace. He reminds her how easily a nurse can be reassigned to the front lines. Emotional beat: power flexing, terror masked as courtesy.

chapters.title: The Mending Circle
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The workshop women—washerwoman Tilda, carpenter Ferro, and old surgeon's assistant Mags—quietly absorb Oscar into their routines, forming an unspoken pact of protection. Emotional beat: found family assembling itself without anyone naming it.

chapters.title: Names in the Ice
chapters.summary: Brannigan's POV. The sergeant, dying slowly of an old wound, asks Jude to add his brother's name to her ledger—the one the officers struck after a failed charge. Emotional beat: grief finding a witness.

chapters.title: An Offer of Silence
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. A major offers Jude money and passage home if she surrenders the boy and forgets what she has written. She refuses, understanding for the first time that her ledger makes her dangerous. Emotional beat: the moment invisibility ends.

chapters.title: Oscar Speaks
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, rendered simply. The boy finally talks, revealing he is the lieutenant's son and heard the order that got his father sent to die. Emotional beat: innocence carrying unbearable testimony.

chapters.title: The Inquiry
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth's POV. The colonel closes the investigation into the lieutenant's death with forged testimony, but learns a ledger exists listing omitted names. His composure cracks. Emotional beat: corruption needing to become violence.

chapters.title: Search of the Workshop
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Soldiers ransack the workshop hunting papers; Jude hides the ledger inside a prosthetic leg Ferro is carving, and they find nothing—but Tilda is arrested on a pretext. Emotional beat: solidarity tested by cost.

chapters.title: What Tilda Carried
chapters.summary: Mags' POV. Tilda, released after three days, refuses to say what was done to her, but she begins teaching Oscar his letters, saying every name must be written somewhere. Emotional beat: endurance as quiet rebellion.

chapters.title: The Thaw Begins
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The river ice groans; orders arrive for the regiment to depart when the water opens, burning all records first. Jude calculates she has weeks to complete the ledger. Emotional beat: the clock starting.

chapters.title: Brannigan's Testimony
chapters.summary: Brannigan's POV. Knowing he will not survive the march, Brannigan dictates a full account of the failed charge and the order that caused it; Jude writes it into the ledger beside his brother's name. Emotional beat: a dying man choosing truth over peace.

chapters.title: Ashworth's Bargain
chapters.summary: Colonel Ashworth's POV. The colonel offers Jude a commission—her own hospital, respectability—if she hands over the ledger and the boy before departure. For one night she genuinely considers it. Emotional beat: temptation of legitimate power.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude declines, telling Ashworth that names are not his to spend. He promises the workshop will burn with everything else. She begins copying the ledger in duplicate, hiding pages in bread loaves and bandage rolls. Emotional beat: resolve hardened into strategy.

chapters.title: Ferro's Last Cabinet
chapters.summary: Ferro's POV. The carpenter builds a false-bottomed medicine chest to carry the ledger and Oscar downstream with a trusted barge pilot, knowing he himself cannot leave without suspicion falling on the others. Emotional beat: sacrifice offered matter-of-factly, like joinery.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Gate
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. A paid informer reveals the escape plan; soldiers seize the chest at the gate and take Oscar to the colonel's quarters. Jude is confined to the workshop. Emotional beat: despair at its lowest point.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Burning
chapters.summary: Multiple short POVs—Mags, Tilda, Ferro, Brannigan. The found family coordinates one last gambit: Mags will drug the guards, Tilda will testify falsely to buy time, Ferro will open the river gate. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into collective courage.

chapters.title: Ice Breaking
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Amid the record-burning chaos, Jude confronts Ashworth in front of assembled officers, reading aloud from memory the names he omitted—including the lieutenant's—and naming Oscar as his witness. The river cracks open behind them. Emotional beat: climax; the invisible made undeniable.

chapters.title: Downstream
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. In the confusion of the thaw and the departing regiment, the plan succeeds: Oscar reaches the barge, the duplicate ledger with him, and Brannigan dies at dawn having seen it done. Jude chooses to go with the boy rather than stay safe. Emotional beat: grief and release intertwined.

chapters.title: Her Own Name
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, epilogue a year later. In a printing shop in a free city, the ledger becomes a published roll of the fallen; Oscar, learning his letters, asks why her name isn't in it. Jude takes the pen and signs the title page. Emotional beat: inheritance reclaimed; history handed back to the people it happened to.
